I mean -- if I can still get a lump in my throat at the sight of a cable car silhouetted against the evening sky atop Nob Hill, or the sound of an audience singing "San Francisco" at the top of its lungs before a movie at the Castro Theatre, just think what it could do for an someone who's never been out of Kansas.
1. It's easy -- everything's new and exciting and amazing -- even that lady with the space-alien lights in her hair that plays the accordian and sings "Feelin' Groovy."
2. You're required by the laws of hospitality to go to all those "tourist" places you'd never dream of visiting on your own (but were secretly dying to see), and you can blame it on your guests.
3. There's nothing quite like seeing your old, familiar haunts through the eyes of a neophyte -- a great way to renew your romance with the city.
With first-timers, itineraries are a little more important than with other types of guests, because there's a lot to squeeze into a day. Tours should be geared around areas where you can park and walk to a number of places, or where there's a logical progression in one direction.
If your virgins are fairly fit and not afraid of a little traipsing, start out early Saturday morning in Chinatown, when the merchants are setting up shop. The streets fill with the smell of simmering soups and barbecue pork buns; in the windows are hanging roast ducks (heads still attached) and bizarre delicacies like armadillo, turtle, and pigs' noses; on the sidewalks are bins of embroidered slippers, wooden toys, and rice-paper candies.
At about 10:30 or 11 a.m., scope out a dim sum parlor. The choices are endless, and it's actually hard to go wrong anywhere in Chinatown, but if your friends are not terribly adventurous, try the Golden Dragon, where you can get all the standards -- pork and shrimp dumplings, roast duck, pot stickers, and sticky rice and sausage wrapped in a lotus leaf.
Location is the prime reason to try the Hang Ah Tea Room, which -- in the tradition of the American "Breakfast Anytime" diner -- serves dim sum until 9 p.m. Billed as the oldest dim sum place in Chinatown (established in 1920 -- the management claims some of the cooks have been here since then), it's located below street level on a tiny back alley called Pagoda Place, at the junction of even tinier Hang Ah Street.
For those who don't like weird food surprises, you can get traditional sweet-and-sour dishes here, as well as dim sum such as shrimp toast, foil-wrapped chicken, and steamed pork buns.
After brunch, wander through Ross Alley, making a requisite stop to watch the little old ladies carefully fold bits of wisdom into wing-shaped cookies at the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, and up to Waverly Place. From the street, these apartment buildings don't look too inviting -- a little rundown, many with locked gates. But look up and it's a whole different world. Incense wafts from the ornate painted balconies, colorful Chinese paper lanterns swing in the breeze. Out-of-towners might feel apprehensive about going inside, but if they can handle four flights of stairs, they'll be rewarded with an amazing vision of pre-twentieth-century Chinese religious life.
Tin Hou Temple, dedicated to the Queen of the Heavens and allegedly the oldest Chinese temple in San Francisco, is the one to visit with neophytes. Step inside the gate, and suddenly you're not in Kansas anymore. The ceiling is festooned with dozens of lanterns hung with red prayer papers and gilded miniature dioramas of villages. On one side, oranges, tangerines, flowers, and incense surround photos of loved ones who've passed away; on the other, there's an altar with ornate antique Buddhas and other intricately carved religious figures. On the balcony, an ancient Chinese woman burns incense and folds prayer papers. Encourage your friends to make a traditional offering by stuffing a dollar or two inside one of the small red envelopes at the front table.

Based on the text material above, generate the response to the following quesion or instruction: Could you recommend a dim sum parlor in Chinatown that serves traditional sweet-and-sour dishes?
Assistant: You can try Hang Ah Tea Room in Chinatown, which serves dim sum until 9 p.m. They also offer traditional sweet-and-sour dishes along with dim sum options such as shrimp toast, foil-wrapped chicken, and steamed pork buns.
User: Could you suggest any other places in Chinatown that I should visit with my first-time visitors?
Assistant: Sure! In addition to the dim sum parlors and the Tin Hou Temple mentioned in the text, there are a few other places you might want to check out with your first-time visitors in Chinatown. For example, you can visit the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory on Ross Alley to watch how fortune cookies are made and even try some fresh ones. You can also walk up and down Grant Avenue, which is the main street in Chinatown, to explore its many shops, markets, and historic landmarks like the Bank of Canton Building and the Chinatown Gate. Another interesting spot is the Chinese Historical Society of America Museum, which showcases the rich history and culture of Chinese Americans in San Francisco and beyond.
User: Can you recommend any walking tours in San Francisco that are suitable for first-time visitors?
Assistant: Yes, there are a lot of walking tours in San Francisco that are great for first-time visitors. Here are a few options you might enjoy:

1. Free Tours by Foot: This company offers a variety of free walking tours of San Francisco, including tours of Fisherman's Wharf, Chinatown, the Mission District, and the Golden Gate Bridge. The tours are tip-based, so you can pay what you think the tour is worth.

2. San Francisco City Guides: This is a volunteer organization that offers over 90 free walking tours of San Francisco's neighborhoods, landmarks, and historic sites. Some popular tours include the Castro, North Beach, and the Palace of Fine Arts.

3. Urban Hiker SF: This company offers unique walking tours of San Francisco's hills and staircases, including tours of Russian Hill, Telegraph Hill, and Twin Peaks. The tours are led by a local guide who shares stories and insights about the city's architecture, history, and culture.

4. Wild SF Tours: This company offers fun and quirky walking tours of San Francisco's counterculture, street art, and literary history. Some popular tours include the "Haight-Ashbury Flower Power Walking Tour" and the "Mission Murals & Mosaics Walking Tour."

These are just a few of the many walking tours available in San Francisco. You're sure to find something that suits your interests and budget!
User: Can you recommend any other places in San Francisco where first-time visitors can experience the city's culture and history?
Assistant: Yes, there are many places in San Francisco that offer unique cultural and historical experiences for first-time visitors. Here are a few you might consider:

1. Alcatraz Island: A must-visit for anyone coming to San Francisco, Alcatraz is a former federal prison that's now a National Historic Landmark. You can take a ferry to the island and explore the prison and its fascinating history.

2. San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA): One of the largest modern art museums in the country, SFMOMA showcases an impressive collection of contemporary and modern art, including works by artists like Frida Kahlo, Andy Warhol, and Jackson Pollock.

3. Golden Gate Park: Spanning over 1,000 acres, Golden Gate Park is a beautiful and expansive park that's home to numerous museums, gardens, and attractions. Visit the de Young Museum to see art and artifacts from around the world, explore the Japanese Tea Garden, or take a stroll through the Music Concourse, a scenic plaza featuring fountains and statues.

4. Cable Cars: One of the most iconic symbols of San Francisco, the city's cable cars offer a fun and unique way to experience the city's hilly streets and historic neighborhoods. Hop on at Union Square and ride to Fisherman's Wharf or take the Powell-Hyde line for stunning views of the bay.

These are just a few examples of the many cultural and historical experiences available in San Francisco. You can also check out local neighborhoods like Chinatown and the Mission District, explore the city's street art scene, or take a historic walking tour to learn more about San Francisco's past.

User: Here is a piece of text: From "San Francisco As You Like It: Over 20 Tailor-Made Tours for Culture Vultures, Shopaholics, Neo-Bohemians, Frenzied Foodies, Savvy Natives, and Everyone Else," to be published in its second edition this spring by Ulysses Press.
Even though I grew up here and can never fully realize the wondrous revelation of seeing San Francisco for the very first time, I imagine that for many it's a life-changing experience. I mean -- if I can still get a lump in my throat at the sight of a cable car silhouetted against the evening sky atop Nob Hill, or the sound of an audience singing "San Francisco" at the top of its lungs before a movie at the Castro Theatre, just think what it could do for an someone who's never been out of Kansas.
1. It's easy -- everything's new and exciting and amazing -- even that lady with the space-alien lights in her hair that plays the accordian and sings "Feelin' Groovy."
2. You're required by the laws of hospitality to go to all those "tourist" places you'd never dream of visiting on your own (but were secretly dying to see), and you can blame it on your guests.
3. There's nothing quite like seeing your old, familiar haunts through the eyes of a neophyte -- a great way to renew your romance with the city.
With first-timers, itineraries are a little more important than with other types of guests, because there's a lot to squeeze into a day. Tours should be geared around areas where you can park and walk to a number of places, or where there's a logical progression in one direction.
If your virgins are fairly fit and not afraid of a little traipsing, start out early Saturday morning in Chinatown, when the merchants are setting up shop. The streets fill with the smell of simmering soups and barbecue pork buns; in the windows are hanging roast ducks (heads still attached) and bizarre delicacies like armadillo, turtle, and pigs' noses; on the sidewalks are bins of embroidered slippers, wooden toys, and rice-paper candies.
At about 10:30 or 11 a.m., scope out a dim sum parlor. The choices are endless, and it's actually hard to go wrong anywhere in Chinatown, but if your friends are not terribly adventurous, try the Golden Dragon, where you can get all the standards -- pork and shrimp dumplings, roast duck, pot stickers, and sticky rice and sausage wrapped in a lotus leaf.
Location is the prime reason to try the Hang Ah Tea Room, which -- in the tradition of the American "Breakfast Anytime" diner -- serves dim sum until 9 p.m. Billed as the oldest dim sum place in Chinatown (established in 1920 -- the management claims some of the cooks have been here since then), it's located below street level on a tiny back alley called Pagoda Place, at the junction of even tinier Hang Ah Street.
For those who don't like weird food surprises, you can get traditional sweet-and-sour dishes here, as well as dim sum such as shrimp toast, foil-wrapped chicken, and steamed pork buns.
After brunch, wander through Ross Alley, making a requisite stop to watch the little old ladies carefully fold bits of wisdom into wing-shaped cookies at the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, and up to Waverly Place. From the street, these apartment buildings don't look too inviting -- a little rundown, many with locked gates. But look up and it's a whole different world. Incense wafts from the ornate painted balconies, colorful Chinese paper lanterns swing in the breeze. Out-of-towners might feel apprehensive about going inside, but if they can handle four flights of stairs, they'll be rewarded with an amazing vision of pre-twentieth-century Chinese religious life.
Tin Hou Temple, dedicated to the Queen of the Heavens and allegedly the oldest Chinese temple in San Francisco, is the one to visit with neophytes. Step inside the gate, and suddenly you're not in Kansas anymore. The ceiling is festooned with dozens of lanterns hung with red prayer papers and gilded miniature dioramas of villages. On one side, oranges, tangerines, flowers, and incense surround photos of loved ones who've passed away; on the other, there's an altar with ornate antique Buddhas and other intricately carved religious figures. On the balcony, an ancient Chinese woman burns incense and folds prayer papers. Encourage your friends to make a traditional offering by stuffing a dollar or two inside one of the small red envelopes at the front table.

c83-m1.summary: The National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC is a massive museum with five floors.
c83-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you summarize what the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC is like? Answer according to: February is arguably the best month of the year. Countless iconic celebrations occur in February: Valentine’s Day, Robyn (Rihanna) Fenty’s birthday, Eat Ice Cream for Breakfast Day, and most importantly, Black History Month. I must preface this article by saying that, if you have never celebrated Black History Month, you should start. It is not exclusive to people of African descent, but rather it is a time for everyone to learn more about all of the amazing people who helped to transform our nation through activism, scholarship, and plain hard work.
This year, to kick off my month-long celebration, I took my first ever trip to the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC. It was incredible. For starters, the museum itself is massive. There are five floors jam packed with timeless artifacts dating as far back as the 13th century all the way to huge influencers of the present such as Oprah Winfrey.
The main attraction of the museum is the humongous concourse that is over a mile long and takes about three hours to complete in one trip. It takes visitors on a journey from the beginnings of slavery in 1400 through the Civil Rights movement of the mid-20th century, up to present day with a theatre showcasing the impact of the Obama family. The entire exhibit is brilliantly laid out, and I now understand why the tickets are so hard to come by.
Apart from the concourse, my favorite exhibit by far was the genealogy room where a professional helps visitors use tools such as ancestry.com and FamilySearch to research your family’s history. After a brief introduction to the technology, visitors are then allotted 30 minutes on the computer to search their family genealogy and send the results to their loved ones. During my visit, I was able to discover both my grandmother’s and great uncle’s original marriage documents and send them to my father. Those documents then led us to find more information about my great grandmother and her origins. Since my visit, my father and I have spent hours on the phone with one another excitedly discussing our roots and the possibility of family members that we have yet to meet.
All in all, I started my Black History Month with a bang and am excited to share the rest of my BHM adventures throughout the month. If you are a Hopkins student, or in the Baltimore area, make sure to keep a look out for all of the Black Heritage Month celebration events we have coming up at JHU Student Affairs.

Same-day passes are also available starting at 6:30 a.m. On a first-come, first-served basis, but these passes often run out quickly. 2. The DuSable Museum of African American History in Chicago, Illinois, which has a collection of more than 15,000 pieces that chronicle the African American experience.

3. The National Civil Rights Museum in Memphis, Tennessee, which is located at the site of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination and has exhibits on the Civil Rights Movement.

4. The Underground Railroad Freedom Center in Cincinnati, Ohio, which is dedicated to the history of the Underground Railroad and its impact on American history.

5. The Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, DC, which has exhibits on the Civil Rights Movement, African American culture, and slavery in America.

These are just a few of the many museums and exhibits across the country that showcase Black History.

c103-m1.source_conv_dialogue:

The last tweet was in response to a fan directly asking if she was referring to Maxine.
In the end, I am not surprised that Maxine is definitely gone, just surprised that an employee would be so vocal about it.
Many times, employees are told to keep quiet to avoid stories like these coming out. Ultimately, Maxine and Anderson must not have eye-to-eye on something, leading to the seamstress's joyful tweets.
Any way you slice it, this was a bold—yet smart—move by Maxine. As she knows the climate of the Diva's division first hand, she may have seen the writing on the wall. Let's face it, the WWE barely has room on TV for the divas they utilize, let alone for those waiting in the wings.
So, Maxine has taken a chance and will test the waters to see where her career winds up. In the end, I applaud her for not just sitting around waiting for the WWE to make a move as many stars do. Instead, she has taken her fate into her own hands, and for better or worse, she will ultimately have some say as to what her future holds.
